name: ความรู้สึกคลานใต้ผิวหนัง
preview_text: ความรู้สึกคลานที่แย่ลงเมื่อมีความเครียด อาการที่ปะทุขึ้นในสภาพอากาศชื้น และอาการเวียนศีรษะและผิวสีซีด มีสามรูปแบบที่แตกต่างกัน โดยแต่ละรูปแบบมี...
categories: ["อาการชาและปัญหาทางประสาทสัมผัส", "ภาวะสมองและระบบประสาท"]
synonyms: ["Tingling or crawling sensations in the limbs", "Skin crawling or ant-walking sensation"]
conventional_description:
Crawling sensations under the skin, medically known as formication or paresthesia, feel like insects crawling on or beneath the skin. They can occur anywhere but are most common in the limbs. Western medicine attributes these sensations to nerve dysfunction, which may result from peripheral neuropathy (due to diabetes, vitamin B12 deficiency, or alcohol use), fibromyalgia, multiple sclerosis, menopause, or anxiety disorders.
Diagnosis typically involves a physical exam, blood tests, and sometimes nerve conduction studies or imaging to rule out underlying conditions. In many cases, no clear cause is found, and the symptom is considered idiopathic.
conventional_treatments: Treatment focuses on managing the underlying condition if identified. For neuropathy, medications like gabapentin, pregabalin, or tricyclic antidepressants may be prescribed. Topical creams containing capsaicin or lidocaine are sometimes used. For menopausal crawling sensations, hormone replacement therapy may be considered. When no cause is found, treatment is symptomatic, often with the same neuropathic pain medications.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, crawling sensations under the skin are understood as a sign that the body's channels and collaterals are not being properly nourished or that something is obstructing the flow of Qi and blood. This can happen because of a deficiency-such as not enough Blood or Essence to moisten the sinews-or because of an excess-such as Phlegm, Dampness, or stagnant Blood blocking the pathways. The sensation is often described as 'ant walking' (蚁行感), and TCM recognizes that its character, location, and triggers reveal the underlying pattern.
The Liver is frequently involved because it stores Blood and governs the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body. When Liver Blood is insufficient, the sinews become dry and unstable, generating internal Wind that causes a crawling, twitching feeling. When Liver Qi stagnates, often from emotional stress, the flow of Qi to the limbs is impaired, leading to intermittent crawling sensations that worsen with frustration.
The Spleen's role in transforming fluids means that if it is weak, Dampness and Phlegm can accumulate and block the channels, creating a heavy, numb crawling. The Kidney stores Essence, which nourishes the brain and marrow; when Essence is depleted, the deep channels lose their nourishment, causing a persistent, deep crawling.
Because the same Western diagnosis can have multiple TCM causes, a thorough assessment is essential. A practitioner will ask about the onset, what makes it better or worse, and accompanying symptoms like dizziness, joint pain, or emotional state. The tongue and pulse then confirm the pattern. This differentiation allows treatment to be precisely targeted-not just to calm the sensation but to correct the root imbalance so it does not return.
classical_quote: 「皮肤如有蚁行状，此由风邪客于腠理，与血气相搏，故令皮肤中如有虫行也。」
classical_translation: "The skin feels as if ants are crawling; this is due to Wind evil lodging in the interstices, struggling with Qi and Blood, causing the sensation of insects moving under the skin."
classical_source:
Zhu Bing Yuan Hou Lun (Treatise on the Origins and Symptoms of Diseases)  ,  Volume 2, Wind Diseases 									·
More references
tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking about the onset and character of the crawling sensation. Is it acute and triggered by weather or infection, or chronic and linked to fatigue or emotions? The answers quickly narrow the field between external invasions like Wind-Damp and internal imbalances such as Liver Qi Stagnation or Blood Deficiency.
If the sensation is recurrent and accompanied by dizziness, dry eyes, muscle twitching, and pale lips, the pattern is likely Liver Wind agitating Internally due to Liver Blood Deficiency. This internal Wind arises because deficient Blood cannot anchor the Liver’s smooth flow, causing the sinews to quiver. The tongue is pale, and the pulse is thin and may feel slightly wiry.
When the crawling feels heavy and numb, as if something is crawling under the skin along with a sense of swelling or muzziness, Phlegm in the Channels is often the culprit. Phlegm-Dampness blocks the meridians, creating a sticky obstruction. The tongue appears swollen with a greasy coating, and the pulse is slippery.
A crawling sensation that worsens with stress, frustration, or emotional upset points to Liver Qi Stagnation. The person may also sigh frequently, feel a tight chest, or experience mood swings. The tongue body is normal or slightly red on the edges, and the pulse is wiry, reflecting the constrained flow of Qi.
If the crawling begins suddenly after exposure to wind and damp weather and is accompanied by skin prickling, joint achiness, and a slight aversion to wind, the pattern is Wind-Damp. This is an external invasion disrupting the superficial channels. The tongue has a thin white coating, and the pulse is floating or soft.
Localized, fixed crawling with a stabbing or boring quality suggests Blood Stagnation. The skin may look darker, and there may be varicose veins or a history of injury. The tongue often shows purple spots, and the pulse is choppy or wiry, indicating obstructed blood flow in the collaterals.
In older or constitutionally weak individuals, a persistent crawling sensation accompanied by lower back soreness, weak knees, tinnitus, and poor memory often points to Kidney Essence Deficiency. The deep reserves are depleted, failing to nourish the brain and channels. The tongue is pale, and the pulse is deep and weak.

patterns.pattern_name: Liver Wind agitating Internally due to Liver Blood Deficiency
patterns.symptoms: ["Crawling or tingling that moves from place to place", "Fine trembling of hands or feet", "Numbness of the limbs", "Dizziness and blurred vision", "Pale or sallow complexion", "Brittle, pale, or ridged nails", "Scanty menstrual periods or absent periods in women"]
patterns.worse_with: Overwork and exhaustion, Emotional stress, Poor or irregular diet, Prolonged standing
patterns.better_with: Rest and good sleep, Warm, nourishing foods, Gentle movement or stretching
patterns.why_this_happens: When Liver Blood is insufficient, the sinews and channels lose their nourishment, becoming dry and brittle. This emptiness creates a vacuum-like instability that stirs up internal Wind, much like a dry, barren landscape generates dust devils. The ungrounded Wind then rushes through the skin and muscles, producing the characteristic shifting, crawling sensations that feel like ants moving under the surface.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, thin, and may tremble when extended; thin white coating. Pulse: fine (Xi) and wiry (Xian), especially at the left Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Liver Blood is easily depleted by overwork, poor nutrition, and emotional strain, which all drain the body's deep reserves. When Blood is insufficient, it cannot anchor the Liver's Yang, and Wind stirs, causing the crawling sensations. Rest, nourishing foods, and gentle movement rebuild Blood and calm the Liver, while stress and exhaustion further deplete it, worsening the internal Wind.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Build Blood with warm, nourishing foods like slow-cooked bone broths, dark leafy greens, red meat, eggs, goji berries, and black sesame. Avoid raw, cold, and depleting foods. Gentle, flowing movement such as tai chi or restorative yoga helps move Qi without exhausting reserves. Prioritize deep sleep and avoid overwork, as the Liver stores Blood and repairs itself during rest.

patterns.pattern_name: Phlegm in the Channels joints and muscles
patterns.symptoms: ["Heavy sensation in the limbs with crawling or numbness", "Joint swelling that feels firm or hard to the touch", "Purplish discolouration of the skin around joints", "Chest tightness and excessive phlegm or mucus", "Stubborn, fixed sensation that does not improve with rest"]
patterns.worse_with: Greasy, heavy foods, Dairy products, Damp or humid weather, Cold exposure, Sedentary lifestyle
patterns.better_with: Gentle movement or stretching, Warmth, Light, easily digestible meals, Warm, dry environment
patterns.why_this_happens: Phlegm is a thick, sticky substance that forms when the body fails to transform fluids properly. When it lodges in the channels and collaterals, it blocks the smooth flow of Qi and blood to the skin and muscles. This obstruction produces abnormal sensations like crawling, tingling, or numbness, often with a heavy, dull ache and stiffness. When Phlegm combines with Blood Stasis, the blockage deepens, making the sensation more stubborn and the skin appear purplish.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: purple body with stasis spots, white greasy coating, distended sublingual veins. Pulse: wiry and choppy, or wiry and slippery if Phlegm predominates.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm and Dampness are heavy, sticky substances that obstruct the channels. Greasy, dairy, and damp-producing foods add to the Phlegm burden, while damp weather invites external Dampness to combine with internal Phlegm, worsening the blockage. Gentle movement and warmth help move Qi and transform Phlegm, while a light diet reduces the raw material for Phlegm production. Keeping dry prevents external Dampness from invading.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, and dairy-rich foods that create Phlegm and Dampness. Eat light, warm meals with plenty of vegetables, and include barley, radish, and tangerine peel to help transform Phlegm. Gentle daily exercise like walking or tai chi keeps Qi and blood moving and prevents stagnation. Keep warm and dry, especially in damp weather.

patterns.why_this_happens:
When Liver Qi stagnates, the free flow of Qi and blood through the body's channels is impaired. This can cause sensations of crawling, tingling, or numbness under the skin, especially in the limbs, because the skin and sinews are not being properly nourished.
The sensation often fluctuates with emotional stress, which is the hallmark of this pattern. It may appear alongside a feeling of distension in the ribs or muscles.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly dark body with red or slightly purple sides, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), taut like a guitar string.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stress and anger cause Qi to stagnate, which blocks the channels and produces the crawling sensation. Movement and relaxation help Qi flow smoothly, alleviating the sensation. Expressing emotions releases the stagnation, while suppressing them worsens it.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Engage in gentle daily exercise like walking or yoga to keep Qi moving. Avoid suppressing emotions; practice deep breathing or meditation. Drink peppermint tea and include citrus fruits and leafy greens in your diet.

patterns.why_this_happens: Wind and Dampness are external pathogens that invade the body's superficial channels. Wind is mobile and unpredictable, while Dampness is heavy and sticky. Together they disrupt the smooth flow of Qi and blood just beneath the skin, leaving the sensory nerves confused and irritable. This is what produces the acute, crawling, prickling sensation that can shift from place to place.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly pale body with a white greasy coating, may be slightly swollen. Pulse: floating (浮 fú) and soggy (濡 rú), sometimes slippery (滑 huá).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind and Dampness are external pathogens that thrive in cold, damp environments and stagnate when the body is still. Warmth and gentle movement help disperse them, while rest allows the body's defensive Qi to recover. Raw and greasy foods create internal Dampness, which makes the external invasion harder to clear.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep warm and dry, especially in damp or windy weather. Eat warm, cooked foods and sip ginger tea. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that create internal Dampness. Gentle daily movement like walking or stretching helps keep Qi and blood moving in the channels.

patterns.why_this_happens: When blood flow becomes sluggish or blocked, the tiny vessels that nourish the skin and muscles cannot deliver fresh blood. This leaves the tissues undernourished and can produce false signals, creating the sensation of something crawling or moving under the skin. The feeling is often fixed in one spot and may be accompanied by a stabbing, pricking pain that worsens with pressure or at night.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: purple or dusky body, stasis spots, distended dark sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: choppy (涩 sè) or wiry (弦 xián).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood Stagnation means blood is not flowing freely. Cold and inactivity congeal blood further, deepening the blockage. Stress tightens the Liver Qi, which can compress vessels and worsen stasis. Warmth and gentle movement, on the other hand, encourage blood to flow smoothly, nourish the skin, and quiet the false crawling signals.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi keeps blood from pooling and congealing. Avoid cold drinks and raw foods, which can thicken and slow blood flow. Cook with modest amounts of warming spices such as turmeric, ginger, and black pepper. Manage stress, because tense Liver Qi can compress vessels and worsen stasis.

patterns.worse_with: Overwork and exhaustion, Excessive sexual activity, Cold, raw foods, Prolonged standing, Emotional stress
patterns.better_with: Rest and good sleep, Warm, nourishing foods, Gentle movement or stretching, Warmth
patterns.why_this_happens: Kidney Essence is the body's most fundamental substance, generating marrow and nourishing the brain, spine, and all channels. When Essence is depleted due to aging, chronic illness, or overwork, the channels and collaterals lose their nourishment. This leads to a deep, persistent crawling sensation under the skin, often felt in the lower back and legs, as the Kidneys' influence extends to the lumbar region and lower limbs. Unlike acute Wind or Dampness, the sensation is dull and chronic, reflecting a profound deficiency rather than an external invasion.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, thin body with little or no coating, possible fine cracks. Pulse: fine, deep, and weak at the rear (chi) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Essence is the body's deepest reserve; overwork, excessive sexual activity, and chronic stress drain it, worsening the malnourishment of channels and the crawling sensation. Rest, warmth, and nourishing foods help to replenish Essence and support circulation, while gentle movement prevents stagnation without further depletion.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warming, nourishing foods such as bone broth, black sesame seeds, walnuts, and goji berries. Prioritize rest and avoid overwork, as exhaustion depletes Essence further. Gentle exercises like Tai Chi or walking can help maintain flow without draining reserves.

faqs.question: Is the crawling sensation a sign of something serious?
faqs.answer: In many cases, crawling sensations are benign and related to stress, fatigue, or a minor imbalance. However, if the sensation appears suddenly with other neurological symptoms like muscle weakness, vision changes, or loss of bladder control, it requires urgent medical evaluation. A TCM practitioner can help determine if the root cause is a simple Qi stagnation or a deeper deficiency.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really stop the crawling feeling?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture works by unblocking the channels and restoring the proper flow of Qi and blood to the affected area. Many people notice a reduction in the intensity and frequency of crawling sensations after just a few sessions, especially when combined with herbal therapy. The key is matching the point selection to the correct TCM pattern.

faqs.question: How long does it take for Chinese herbs to work?
faqs.answer: Most patients begin to feel a difference within 2-4 weeks of taking a properly prescribed herbal formula. Acute, externally triggered patterns may respond in days, while chronic, deficiency-based patterns often require several months of consistent use to rebuild the body's reserves. It's important to take the herbs as directed and not stop prematurely.

faqs.question: Can I combine TCM with my nerve pain medication?
faqs.answer: Generally, yes, but you must inform both your TCM practitioner and your prescribing doctor. Some herbs that move Blood (such as Dang Gui or Chuan Xiong) may interact with blood thinners, and sedative herbs could amplify the effects of gabapentin or antidepressants. Never stop or adjust your medication without medical supervision.

faqs.question: Will the crawling sensation come back after treatment?
faqs.answer: When the root imbalance is fully corrected, the sensation should not return. However, if the lifestyle or emotional factors that triggered it persist, there is a risk of recurrence. TCM practitioners often recommend periodic maintenance treatments and dietary adjustments to sustain the results long-term.

faqs.question: Does diet affect this sensation?
faqs.answer: Yes. In TCM, cold, raw, and greasy foods can weaken the Spleen and generate Dampness or Phlegm, which can worsen crawling sensations. A warm, nourishing diet rich in cooked vegetables, soups, and moderate amounts of lean protein supports Blood and Qi and helps prevent recurrence. Reducing sugar, dairy, and alcohol is often advised.

faqs.question: Is it safe to treat during pregnancy?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture by a licensed practitioner is generally safe during pregnancy, and many points can be used to relieve crawling sensations. However, certain acupuncture points and herbs are contraindicated in pregnancy. Always inform your practitioner if you are pregnant or trying to conceive so they can adjust the treatment accordingly.

research.title: Acupuncture for diabetic peripheral neuropathy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This systematic review pooled data from 15 RCTs and found that acupuncture significantly improved nerve conduction velocity and reduced symptoms of numbness, tingling, and pain compared to conventional medication alone. Although crawling sensations were not specifically isolated, the overall improvement in sensory symptoms suggests benefit for formication as part of the neuropathic picture.
research.periodical: Chen W, Yang GY, Liu B, et al. Acupuncture for diabetic peripheral neuropathy: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Diabetes Research. 2019;2019:1-12.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicine for diabetic peripheral neuropathy: a systematic review
research.description: This review included 22 RCTs evaluating various Chinese herbal formulas. The meta-analysis showed that herbal medicine combined with conventional treatment was more effective than conventional treatment alone in improving sensory nerve function and reducing paresthesia symptoms. Commonly used herbs included Huang Qi, Dang Gui, and Chuan Xiong.
research.periodical: Zhang Y, Li J, Wang X. Chinese herbal medicine for diabetic peripheral neuropathy: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine. 2020;2020:1-10.

research.title: Acupuncture for chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy: a randomized clinical trial
research.description: This pilot RCT of 60 patients with chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy found that real acupuncture significantly reduced neuropathic pain and paresthesia scores at 8 weeks compared to sham acupuncture. The crawling and tingling sensations were among the secondary outcomes that showed improvement.
research.periodical: Lu W, Giobbie-Hurder A, Freedman RA, et al. Acupuncture for chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA Oncology. 2020;6(2):271-278.
